message:
QUESTION:
Did guard X's three-point shooting genuinely improve after the mid-season change of shooting coach, and should X take a larger share of the team's three-point attempts next season?

DATA:
Professional basketball. Guard X's shooting before and after a mid-season change of shooting coach, which took effect after game 30. X played in all 50 games. His minutes per game were similar in both periods (about 32).

Shooting percentage = makes / attempts.

| | Games 1-30 | Games 31-50 |
| Three-point attempts | 150 | 80 |
| Three-point makes | 51 | 32 |
| Free-throw attempts | 100 | 70 |
| Free-throw makes | 80 | 55 |

League average three-point percentage this season: 36%.

Opponent breakdown: in games 31-50, 30 of X's 80 three-point attempts came in 4 games against the league's two worst-ranked perimeter defences, and he made 18 of those 30. X did not face either of those teams in games 1-30.

The coaching staff must decide whether to increase X's share of team three-point attempts next season. The new shooting coach worked with the whole squad, not just X.

<analysis>
# Receipt

**1. Take the change log out of the report (must fix).** The previous version began with a "Receipt" about a draft and a reviewer that the coaching staff never saw. It also included working notes such as "I checked this." Ironically, its own first point said draft references should go. **Change:** the report below starts at its title and contains no revision history. This Receipt is a separate note for whoever asked for the revision. It is not part of what goes to the staff.

**2. The 32.5% figure is a floor, not an equal end of the range.** Removing only the two worst defences strips out the easiest part of X's schedule. It leaves every other weak team in, and every real schedule contains weak teams. Four of 50 games against those two teams may be about normal. Also, with only 230 attempts, a sensible estimate of his true rate is pulled strongly toward the league average. **Change:** the best estimate becomes "roughly league average, about 35–36%." 32.5% is described as a conservative floor. The recommendation does not change.

**3. The decision trigger uses the wrong benchmark and will arrive late.** The decision concerns X's share of the team's attempts, so the comparison should be X against the teammates whose shots he would take, not just the league's 36%. Also, 250–300 attempts at 4–5 per game is about 55–65 games, which is most of next season. **Change:** the trigger now names the teammate comparison. It notes that comparing two noisy rates needs a larger gap or more data. It also warns staff that the trigger cannot fire early.

**4. Don't imply X got worse.** Section 1 said he was "6 points worse than before the change." But 28% on 50 attempts against 34% on 150 has a standard error of about 7.4 points, so that drop is noise too. **Change:** Section 1 now flags the drop as within noise.

**Minor.**
- Free throws are only weakly related to three-point skill. **Change:** they are kept as a weak supporting check, worded "reasonable, if imperfect," and given no more weight.
- The team-level before/after test is the most useful next step. **Change:** it moves up to the summary and to first place in the recommendations.

**Unchanged:** all figures. I rechecked the new 7.4-point standard error and the 55–65 game estimate. Both answers stand: there is no reliable evidence of genuine improvement, and no case on these data for giving X a larger share of three-point attempts.

---

# Guard X: Three-Point Shooting Since the Coaching Change

## Summary

The data do not show that X's three-point shooting genuinely improved after the change of shooting coach. They do not support giving him a larger share of the team's three-point attempts next season.

His raw percentage rose from 34.0% to 40.0%, but three facts undercut that rise:

- **The gain is accounted for by weak opponents.** The rise comes entirely from 30 attempts against the league's two weakest perimeter defences, teams he did not face before game 30. Against all other opponents he shot 28% after the change. Like the headline gain, that figure is within normal variation.
- **The gap is within normal variation.** Even before adjusting for opponents, a 6-point difference on these sample sizes is easily produced by chance.
- **Free throws did not improve.** His free-throw percentage fell slightly, from 80.0% to 78.6%. This is a weak check, but it gives no sign of better mechanics.

The best current estimate of X's ability is roughly league average, about 35–36%. A conservative floor is about 32.5%.

The most useful next step is to test the coaching change at team level. The new coach worked with the whole squad, so the team's before/after three-point figures, split by opponent strength, would be far stronger evidence than one player's 80 attempts.

## Data and context

- The season is split at game 30, when the new shooting coach took over. The coach works with the whole squad, not only X.
- X played all 50 games, at about 32 minutes per game in both periods. Changes in playing time therefore do not explain any difference.
- Shooting percentage = makes ÷ attempts.

| | Games 1–30 | Games 31–50 | Season |
|---|---|---|---|
| Three-point makes / attempts | 51 / 150 | 32 / 80 | 83 / 230 |
| Three-point % | 34.0% | 40.0% | 36.1% |
| Three-point attempts per game | 5.0 | 4.0 | 4.6 |
| Free-throw makes / attempts | 80 / 100 | 55 / 70 | 135 / 170 |
| Free-throw % | 80.0% | 78.6% | 79.4% |

League average three-point percentage: 36%.

## 1. The headline improvement is driven by opponents

In games 31–50, 30 of X's 80 attempts came in 4 games against the two worst-ranked perimeter defences. He made 18 of them. He did not play either team in games 1–30, so the two periods faced different opposition.

| Games 31–50 | Games | Makes / attempts | % | Attempts per game |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| vs two worst perimeter defences | 4 | 18 / 30 | 60.0% | 7.5 |
| vs all other opponents | 16 | 14 / 50 | 28.0% | 3.1 |
| Total | 20 | 32 / 80 | 40.0% | 4.0 |

The "all other opponents" group is the one most comparable to his games 1–30 schedule. Against it X shot 28%, against 34% before the change. That drop is also within noise: on 50 versus 150 attempts the standard error of the difference is about 7.4 points. It is not evidence that he got worse.

Likewise, the 60% figure rests on only 30 shots over 4 games and is not his true level against weak defences. The point is simply that the aggregate 40% reflects the schedule, not a better shooter.

## 2. Even the raw difference is within chance

Set the opponent split aside. A rise from 34.0% (150 attempts) to 40.0% (80 attempts) has a standard error of about 6.7 percentage points. The 6-point gain is therefore less than one standard error, well within what random variation produces.

A true 36% shooter would quite often post a 34% stretch followed by a 40% stretch over samples this size. Three-point percentage needs several hundred attempts to stabilise, and the post-change sample is 80.

The honest conclusion is not that X got better or worse. Once opponents are accounted for, nothing in these data distinguishes his shooting after the change from his shooting before it.

## 3. Free throws: a weak check, but no sign of change

X's free-throw percentage moved from 80.0% (80/100) to 78.6% (55/70). On 70 attempts that change is too small to mean anything.

Free throws are a reasonable, if imperfect, check on shooting technique, because they are uncontested and taken from a fixed spot. They are only loosely related to three-point skill, so this is supporting evidence at most. It gives no sign of a mechanical improvement.

## 4. Other points to note

**Volume and opponents.** X's attempts fell from 5.0 to 4.0 per game at the same minutes. The split shows this was not a move toward fewer, better shots:
- Against the weakest defences he took 7.5 attempts per game and shot well.
- Against everyone else he took about 3.1 per game, down from 5.0 before the change.

One possible reading is that normal defences were limiting his looks. These data cannot confirm that, and they say nothing about how his efficiency would change at higher volume.

**Which baseline to plan around.**
- His full-season rate is 36.1%. With 4 of 50 games against the two weakest defences, that may be close to a normal schedule.
- On only 230 attempts, a sensible estimate of his true ability is pulled toward the league average anyway.
- The best planning figure is therefore roughly league average, about 35–36%.
- Excluding the 30 attempts against the weakest defences gives 32.5% (65/200). Treat this as a conservative floor, not an equally likely outcome, because it removes only the easiest games and leaves every other weak opponent in.

**Expected value.** At 36% an X three is worth about 1.08 points per attempt, the same as a league-average three. At the 32.5% floor it is about 0.98. Whether moving attempts from teammates to X would add points depends on how those teammates compare, which these data do not show.

## Recommendation

1. **Test the coaching effect at team level first.** Compare the squad's three-point percentage before and after game 30, split by opponent strength.
   - If the whole team improved against comparable opponents, that is meaningful evidence the coach is helping.
   - If only X's numbers rose, and only against weak defences, that points to the schedule and to chance.
   - Where tracking data exist, also compare shot quality: contested versus open, and catch-and-shoot versus off-the-dribble.
2. **Do not increase X's share of team three-point attempts on the strength of this data.** Plan around him as roughly a league-average three-point shooter (about 35–36%), with about 32.5% as a conservative floor.
3. **Keep collecting evidence.** Continue X's work with the new coach. Reassess once he has a few hundred post-change attempts against a representative range of opponents.
4. **Set a concrete decision trigger in advance, and expect it to take time.**
   - **Benchmark.** Compare X with the teammates whose attempts he would take, on opponent-adjusted three-point percentage, not only with the 36% league average.
   - **Size of gap.** After about 250–300 further attempts, the standard error on X's own rate will be about 2.9 points. Against a fixed 36% benchmark, he would need about 40–41% before the gap is clearly real. A comparison with teammates carries noise on both sides, so it needs a somewhat larger gap or more attempts. Rates a point or two above the benchmark are still within noise.
   - **Timing.** At 4–5 attempts per game, 250–300 attempts takes about 55–65 games, most of next season. The trigger cannot fire early.
   - **Streaks.** Do not reward or penalise him on short streaks in either direction.
</analysis>

Produce the final version of this analysis.
